author: The Canadian Press
title: Denied Indigenous rights, NunatuKavut council fighting Canada in Federal Court
content:
The NunatuKavut Community Council in Labrador is fighting Canada’s decision to deny the group Indigenous rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.




In a Federal Court application, the council says the Canadian government ignored historical and genealogical evidence when it ended Indigenous rights talks with the group last month.




Dated late last week, the application seeks to quash the government’s decision to abandon talks with the council.




The NunatuKavut Community Council says it represents about 6,000 Inuit in southern and central Labrador, though it is not recognized by other Inuit groups, including the Inuit Nunatsiavut government in northern Labrador.




Last month, Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada said information provided by the council did not meet established tests for rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.




Section 35 of the Constitution Act recognizes and affirms Indigenous and treaty rights.




In a news release Monday, the community council said it received “affirming messages and feedback” from Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada about its claim for rights. The department told the council it had met a test to proceed to land claim negotiations,

 the release said.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Proposed bill would push RCMP to enforce First Nations law
content:
The Senate committee on national defence began the study of a proposed bill that would make RCMP officers enforce bylaws enacted by First Nation governments.




“Why we are here is to fight for the same rights that other Canadians have and we don’t,” said Sen. Mary Jane McCallum, sponsor of Bill S-223.




The 

proposed law

, 

An Act to Amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act

, is meant to ensure that the duties of the RCMP would “include the prevention of offences against First Nation laws and the execution of warrants that may, under First Nation laws, be lawfully executed and performed by peace officers,” according to the bill.




This means that bylaws passed by First Nations governments that are regularly published in the 

First Nations Gazette

 — a national government resource for announcements and updates from leadership — would be enforced by RCMP with the same urgency as a municipal or provincial law.




Bylaws are laws that are established by municipal governments or corporations and apply to only a specific jurisdiction.




According to Jennifer Ebert, assistant commissioner of operational policing services at the RCMP, First Nations can make bylaws under the Indian Act, but the legislation does not specify who is responsible for enforcing them.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Health minister calls alcohol ‘one of the major concerns’ for Indigenous communities
content:
The federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel says she’s aware of Sen. Patrick Brazeau’s bill to put cancer warnings on alcohol and that she has already spoken with him about it.




Michel made the comments Monday at the Sheraton Hotel in Ottawa, after a press conference with Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty and Lucy Kuptana, the Northwest Territories’ interim minister of health and social services.




The event announced $51.2 million over seven years for primary care and mental health in the Northwest Territories, plus more than $100 million to build or repair health facilities in 12 communities.




Asked whether Brazeau’s Bill S-202 was on her radar, Michel said she’s “looking into it.”




“I know about the bill, and I also spoke with the senator,” she said. “Alcohol is already a recognized harm; for Indigenous communities it was one of the major concerns for years. So yes, we are looking into it.”




Asked about the impact of alcohol on the health-care system and on addictions, Michel said, “To be honest, I don’t have the exact impact; we know people are suffering with addiction, but on alcohol specifically I don’t have it.”




The answer is the first the minister has given APTN on the bill. In March, APTN asked Michel the same question, but, after repeated attempts, she refused to answer questions on whether she supports warning labels.

author: Dennis Ward
title: Mandy Gull-Masty’s balancing act as Indigenous Services minister
content:
Over the past year and a half, Mandy Gull-Masty says a lot of people have asked, “Why is it that you chose to become the Indian agent?”




In May 2025, Gull-Masty, the first ever woman to be elected as the grand chief of the Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee), became the first ever Indigenous person to head up Indigenous Services Canada (ISC).




The minister says she wants to support the vision of First Nations and “give them the tools they need so that they can take the space of determining how they want services delivered and ultimately doing the work of delivering those services, themselves.”




Gull-Masty admits the job comes with “a lot of balancing, a lot of stress, a lot of moments of quiet thought and deep reflection” and that she is “trying to maintain who she is.”




Gull-Masty has a number of high profile issues on her plate, including the reintroduction of the 

First Nations Clean Water Act.




Another controversial piece of legislation is Bill S-2.




The government of Prime Minister Mark Carney has been accused of stalling on ending 

the second-generation cut-off.




Consultation on Bill S-2 wrapped up in July.




While many in leadership have called for Parliament to pass the legislation, Gull-Masty says she’s trying to reflection everyone’s voice.

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon government asks court to dismiss lawsuit launched by Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in First Nation
content:
The Yukon government denies it breached its duty to consult with a First Nation that launched a lawsuit against it earlier this year, according to a statement of defence filed in the Supreme Court of Yukon last week.




The Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in First Nation, based in Dawson City about a six-and-a-half hour’s drive north of Whitehorse, 

launched the legal action against the government on Jan. 28.




The lawsuit claims the government didn’t consult with it before making 

temporary regulatory amendments to the territory’s mining regulations last year

 to ease a backlog of mining authorizations.




The suit accuses the government of failing or refusing to provide adequate resources and staffing to address a “foreseeable surge” of mining application renewals, enabling it to acquire “significant savings.”




It also alleges the government “relaxed” regulatory mining requirements, including those under the territory’s Waters Act and Quartz Mining Act, which allowed projects needing new authorizations to continue. The suit claims that permitted projects to proceed “without strict compliance” and with “expired plans.”




Those amendments, it claims, violated its Final Agreement.




It argues that the government breached its duty to consult and accommodate the First Nation by failing to give it “reasonable advance notice” ahead of the amendments, among other things.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Don’t mistake attendance at a press conference as support for a pipeline, chief says
content:
The grand chief of Treaty 8 First Nations stood behind Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last week as they announced the 

Pacific Link pipeline

 was the first project deemed to be in the “national interest” under the Building Canada Act.




But Trevor Mercredi said his presence shouldn’t be taken as a vote of confidence.




“I want to be clear that our presence should not be interpreted as support for the project,” Mercredi told The Canadian Press.




“Leadership was there to ensure our nations are not left behind. There are significant concerns that must be addressed, and it does not mean the pipeline is a done deal.”




The national interest designation under the Building Canada Act, puts the pipeline proposal in line for streamlined oversight and approvals.




The government said it will work over the coming year to complete consultations on the project itself, and to secure environmental safeguards, financing and Indigenous partnerships. It wants construction to begin in September 2027.




Some 130 Indigenous communities were given just two months for consultations on whether the pipeline should be granted a national interest designation, and that was still more than the government had planned.

title: Woman charged with murder of Liard First Nation man in Watson Lake, Yukon
content:
A woman in southeast Yukon has been charged with second-degree murder in the death of a First Nations man.




Jennifer Jules, 37, of Watson Lake, is accused of killing Alvin Stone.




APTN News confirmed Stone was from Liard First Nation.




According to a 

statement from the RCMP

, officers responded to a call reporting “an injured man” in Watson Lake.




Jules was already facing charges from an alleged assault on Aug. 12 involving a torch lighter.




Her next court date is Oct. 15 in Whitehorse.




She remains in custody.

author: Stéphanie de Sève
title: 350 km à pied et à pagaie : une expédition pour la réconciliation
content:
C’est sur le territoire anishnabe de la communauté de Kitigan Zibi que l’expédition Mamu Nikantetau a débuté, cette année. Une traversée qui se veut une rencontre entre des participants de différentes nations et des allochtones.




Initiée par le Dr Stanley Vollant, l’expédition en est à sa 4e édition. Pour le Dr Vollant, « la réconciliation doit être plus qu’un simple mot ou un concept. » Mamu Nikantetau en innu veut dire « avançons ensemble ». Cette année, l’aventure s’est déroulée à pied mais surtout en rabaska pour un total de 350 kilomètres.




Un an avant l’expédition, Guylaine Gros-Louis s’entraînait déjà dans l’espoir de se joindre au groupe. Elle a appris la bonne nouvelle en juillet et s’est munie d’un entraîneur privé pour travailler le haut de son corps : « C’est la fierté de faire ce périple-là, c’est un dépassement de soi. »




« Si je peux être un exemple, une source de motivation pour d’autres personnes, pourquoi pas. »




Derrière sa participation se cache une quête d’équilibre des quatre sphères : « il y a des sphères qui sont plus fragilisées, puis c’est d’aller travailler là-dessus. »




Une marche symbolique a marqué le début de cette aventure de dix jours.




Dr Vollant : « une 2e journée plus chargée avec une traversée de la rivière des Outaouais, appelée la kichi sibi et occupée par les communautés anishnabee depuis des millénaires. »




Rencontré

author: Mike McDonald
title: ISC minister, chief of Namaygoosisagagun First Nation meet to discuss rebuild
content:
A recent meeting between Namaygoosisagagun First Nation (Collins Lake) and the minister of Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) left the chief with questions.




“What are we rebuilding?” Helen Paavola told APTN News of the Sept. 29 meeting with Minister Mandy Gull-Masty. “And that is a good question. What are we rebuilding? Are we just going back to what our community was? How many structures? So, they’re very good questions.”




In July, community members barely escaped with their lives after a wildfire swept in. People escaped in boats and posted dramatic photos on social media of their flight.




Namaygoosisagagun isn’t under the Indian Act, so unlike other First Nations, the millions needed to rebuild wasn’t guaranteed.




The community has been negotiating its status with the federal government since 2018.




Gull-Masty told APTN that Ottawa will help – but the community needs to come up with some answers.




“What kind of support does she need? How do you work with your members to define how that rebuild is going to look like? And, most importantly, how do you support them through also living through a very traumatic experience of losing the community?” Gull-Masty said.




The summer of 2026 saw some of the worst wildfires in recorded history. A number of communities in northern Ontario had to evacuate because of oncoming flames and smoke.

author: Cierra Bettens
title: Beyond the ballot: Why the Alberta referendum is about more than separation
content:
On Oct. 19, 

Albertans will vote

 on whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process to hold a binding provincial referendum on separation from Canada.




They’ll also be answering “yes” or “no” to nine additional questions, ranging from immigration to abolishing the Canadian Senate.




This week on APTN News InFocus, journalist Danielle Paradis joins us to dig deeper into the Alberta referendum.




Paradis spent the summer travelling across Alberta with journalist Tim Querengesser for their podcast, Separation Anxiety. They found themselves in church boardrooms and hot dog picnics, talking to organizers about the roots of the separatist movement.




When it comes to understanding Indigenous sovereignty and Treaty rights, Paradis said Albertans are generally “no different from the rest of Canada”.




“You just don’t see people understanding that the First Nations understand this as an agreement to share the land. Not ceding the land, but that there is this acknowledgement that we’re going to be living together, that we have this ongoing relationship,” Paradis said.




“It’s all of a sudden apparent that there are some real rights for the land and power that the First Nations communities hold when it comes to whether or not Alberta would get to separate.”

title: « La vie est un choix difficile » : un chirurgien innu termine un parcours de 350 km à la pagaie avec des jeunes et des aînés
content:
Avertissement : cet article parle de suicide et d’abus sexuels.




La foule rassemblée autour du canal Lachine, au sud du centre-ville de Montréal, a éclaté en acclamations et en applaudissements lorsque les quatre rabaskas (grands canoës de style algonquin) se sont approchés de la rive, marquant ainsi la fin du périple de 350 km de l’

expédition Mamu Nikantetau

Le groupe est parti de la nation algonquine de Kitigan Zibi, a descendu jusqu’à Ottawa, puis s’est rendu dans les communautés mohawks de Kanehsatà:ke et Kahnawà:ke, avant d’atteindre sa destination : Montréal.

author: APTN National News
title: NDP MP calls for emergency debate over White nationalism, anti-Indigenous racism
content:
On the heels of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, NDP MP Leah Gazan (Winnipeg Centre) is calling for an emergency debate in the House of Commons over White nationalism and anti-Indigenous racism.




“There is an urgent need for an Emergency Debate to allow Parliamentarians to respond to the attacks on the truth of what happened in residential schools, the escalating attacks that pose a grave threat to the physical and psychological safety of survivors, families and our nations,” Gazan wrote to the Speaker of the House of Commons Francis Scarpaleggia.




Days before the NDTR, a white nationalist organization called the Second Sons of Canada showed on Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc (TteS) territory. The participants who all had their faces covered, later hung a banner across a local bridge that read “Got Bones?” in reference to the 215 anomalies identified beside the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.




Gazan called the display, “a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division.”




“The statement on the banner is a reference to the 

disproven 

“mass grave hoax” conspiracy – an overt form of residential school denialism, seeking to dismiss established evidence and erase documented history of a genocide recognized unanimously by the House of Commons in 2022.”

author: Meral Jamal
title: Facing wildfires, permafrost thaw and flooding, Northern community leaders say security announcements will help
content:
Editor’s note: This story is the first in a series, supported by the Pulitzer Center and co-published by Canadian Geographic and APTN News.







Peter Clarkson has been the mayor of the town of Inuvik twice.




His first term was between 2000 and 2006. He had moved to the community, in the Inuvialuit Settlement Region of the Northwest Territories, over two decades prior to work as a wildlife biologist, focusing on wolves, caribou and grizzly bears. In that role, he supported the development of a co-management system for both the Inuvialuit and Gwich’in following their land claims settlements in the region.




He also worked as the director of the Gwich’in Renewable Resource Board during this time and with the territorial government in the years following. In the community, he helped launch key initiatives including the development of the local greenhouse and getting the Mackenzie Valley fibre off the ground.




Roughly 40 years after he first moved to the town, Clarkson was elected mayor for a second term in October 2024. In the time since, he says he has found himself in discussions about development in Inuvik of a different nature: infrastructure announcements supporting the federal government and the military in their plans for Arctic security.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Tentative settlement in First Nation class action over non-consensual MRI scans
content:
A tentative settlement has been reached in a class action lawsuit alleging that members of 

Pictou Landing First Nation

 in Nova Scotia underwent MRI scans without their consent.




The law firm representing the class confirmed Thursday that the proposed settlement with the defendants — two Halifax doctors — is subject to approval from the Nova Scotia Supreme Court.




None of the allegations in the lawsuit have been tested in court.




The original lawsuit, filed in 2020 and certified in 2024, alleged that radiologists Robert Miller and Sharon Clarke took magnetic resonance imaging scans of about 60 members of the Pictou Landing First Nation without their knowledge or consent.




A statement of claim filed in Nova Scotia Supreme Court says band members agreed to undergo the scans as part of a research project in 2017 but were subjected to additional “secret” scans of their livers for a separate study.




The lawsuit alleged the defendants were liable for invasion of privacy, acting recklessly and causing distress and anguish. They were also accused of negligence, unlawful imprisonment and assault and battery for allegedly keeping the participants inside the confined space of the MRI machine for longer than they should have.




The lawsuit also accused them of failing to advise participants of serious health issues that were discovered on the scans.

author: Sara Connors
title: Parole board revokes statutory release for man convicted of killing two First Nations women
content:
The man convicted of killing two First Nations women in Winnipeg over a decade ago is back in custody less than a year after he was granted statutory release.




The 

Parole Board of Canada

 revoked 66-year-old’s Shawn Lamb’s statutory release last week.




In the board’s written decision, it noted Lamb breached multiple conditions of his release. It also highlighted issues about his behaviour and conduct, ultimately determining he posed an “undue risk” to society.




“There are concerns that you have re-entered your offence cycle,” it states.




Originally charged with second-degree murder in the killings of Carolyn Sinclair, 25, Lorna Blacksmith, 18, and Tanya Nepinak, 31, Lamb pleaded guilty to manslaughter in Sinclair and Blacksmith’s deaths. The charge in Nepinak’s death was stayed due to a lack of evidence.




He was sentenced to 20 years in federal prison in 2013, minus two years’ credit for time served.




By law, most federal inmates are released on statutory release after serving two-thirds of their sentence. Similar to parole, offenders serve the remaining third of their sentence in the community under supervision.




Lamb was released on statutory release in November 2025.




At the time, the board imposed special conditions on his release, including that he reside at a community-based residential centre, not consume drugs and report relationships.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Manitoba’s handling of moose hunting an ‘infringement’ on Treaty rights: court documents
content:
A First Nation in northern Manitoba is taking the province back to court over its handling of big game licenses, claiming it infringes on Treaty rights and prior hunting agreements.




Leadership at Pimicikamak First Nation, also known as Cross Lake, claims its members should, but do not have, priority when it comes to hunting the dwindling population of moose on its traditional territory.




This is after a judge “misapprehended” a request for judicial review on Manitoba’s handling of moose hunting in 2024, according to court documents.




And while the matter is not settled, the community is also calling upon hunters to hand their licenses back for the rest of the 2026-2027 season to give the animals a chance to recover.




Pimicikamak, located approximately 520 kilometres north of Winnipeg, sits in the boreal forest and consists of approximately 10,400 hectares of land.




It’s part of 

Game-Hunting Area (GHA) 9A

, which, according to Manitoba’s most recent air survey results collected in 2025, only has an estimated tally of 599 moose over 35,608 square kilometers.




According to the 

Manitoba Wildlife Federation (MWF)

, the area’s bull moose population has declined by 53 per cent over the last decade.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Mi’kmaw lawyer says Ottawa is stalling on ending second-generation cut-off
content:
Nine months after the Senate voted unanimously to end the second-generation cut-off, the federal government must now decide what to do with Bill S-2.

The government bill was introduced in the Senate, where senators added an amendment the government wasn’t expecting and doesn’t want.

The amendment would force Ottawa to scrap the second-generation cut-off and replace it with a one-parent rule.

Pam Palmater, Mi’kmaw lawyer and chair in Indigenous governance at Toronto Metropolitan University, has testified on a number of occasions at federal committees on the issue.

“Every single First Nation person is affected by Bill C-31 and the second-generation cut-off,” Palmater told APTN News.

Bill C-31, passed in 1985, split people registered under the Indian Act into two legal classes.

A person under section 6(1) of the law can pass status to a child no matter who the other parent is. But a person under section 6(2) — “one parent” status — can pass it on only if the other parent is also registered as “status” under the Indian Act.

After two generations of parenting with someone who is not registered, the third generation is out. That is the second-generation cut-off.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: ‘Life is a difficult choice’: Innu surgeon completes 350 km paddle with youth, Elders
content:
Warning: This story discusses suicide and sexual abuse.




The crowd surrounding the Lachine Canal just south of downtown Montreal broke into cheers and applause as the four rabaskas (large Algonquin-style canoes) approached the shore, bringing an end to the 350 km journey of this year’s 

Mamu Nikantetau expedition

 on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.




Led by Dr. Stanley Vollant, an Innu from Pessamit and the first Indigenous person to become a surgeon in Quebec, the 5th Mamu Nikantetau expedition brought together 29 mostly Indigenous participants.




The group travelled from the Algonquin Nation of Kitigan Zibi, down to Ottawa and then to  the Mohawk communities of Kanehsatake and Kahnawake, before reaching their final destination of Montreal.




“People don’t know each other at all at the beginning,” Vollant told APTN News. “They have to talk, they have to know each other, they have to know their past, their trauma, what they are heading for and their objective, and then we have to respect each other, respect the differences.”




For the expedition to succeed, he explained, the group must figure out everyone’s strengths and weaknesses and get to know one another well enough that they can work together to achieve the common goal of carrying the voyage through to its end.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: West Coast chiefs join First Nations along Pacific Link pipeline in denouncing government over lack of consultation
content:
The Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs (UBCIC) is promising to fight against the west coast Pacific Link pipeline designated to be in the “national interest” by Prime Minister Mark Carney today.




“We have a duty and an obligation to protect our rights to the fullest extent of the law and we have every intention of doing that. This is not a cake walk, this is not a ‘gimme’, this will be hard-fought in the court rooms, and if necessary, with boots on the ground,” said UBCIC president Grand Chief Stewart Phillip.




Phillip joins a growing chorus of First Nation voices speaking out against Pacific Link.




Five other west coast chiefs spoke out about the pipeline in a late afternoon news release.




“We demand that the legal principle of ‘free, prior, informed consent’ enshrined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act and the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act be fully engaged in ‘all’ fast-tracked projects sponsored by the Major Projects Office,” Phillip said. He called the Pacific Link pipeline unique and that it has tossed aside “fundamental pillars” of Canada’s relationship with First Nations.




Heiltsuk K̓áwáziɫ Chief Marilyn Slett, stated, “At the heart of our fight is keeping our coast super tanker free and protected from jeopardizing our way of life, economy and future. Whether the tankers travel south or north it’s all t

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Carney offers First Nations 10% stake in Pacific Link pipeline, designates it as project of ‘national interest’
content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney stood with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Thursday and listed a new oil pipeline to the southern British Columbia coast — now called Pacific Link — as a project of national interest, the first to get that designation under the Building Canada Act.




Ottawa says Indigenous communities will be offered a minimum 10 per cent ownership interest, financed through Canada and Alberta’s Indigenous loan guarantee programs.




Carney said the designation is how Canada stops waiting years on major projects




“Canada has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become a global energy superpower,” he said in a statement issued with the announcement. “Pacific Link is critical to this mission. To seize this opportunity, we are building together — boldly, sustainably, and in true partnership with Indigenous Peoples.”




According to the government, Canada and Alberta will share equal ownership while Pembina Pipeline Corporation is a private-sector investor. Development is being led by the federally owned Trans Mountain Corporation, the company that built the existing line to the West Coast.




According to the government, there is no schedule to start. It moves the project into a single federal review, led by the MPO and backed by the Canada Energy Regulator. Ottawa wants a conditions document — covering ownership, benefits, Indigenous rights, environmental pro

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Educators say introducing kids to reconciliation requires kinship, cultural approach
content:
When it comes to educating kids about truth and reconciliation, several educators in Winnipeg are approaching the subject with an air of culture, rather than caution.




To mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (NDTR), several organizations offered educational opportunities for families to engage with survivors, knowledge keepers, and Indigenous teachers to learn more about the outstanding impact of residential schools, as well as engage with First Nations cultures and storytelling.




When it comes to what occurred at residential schools, parents, teachers and relatives are often tasked with the challenge of approaching the subject in a way that does not cause further harm.




The Kapabamayak Achaak Healing Forest in Winnipeg, which saw approximately 600 students the week of the NDTR this year, handles the responsibility in a variety of ways.




The forest, which is centred by a gathering space with room for a sacred fire, was established in 2016 and has since been a community resource and “living memorial,” 

according to its website

, “to honour Indigenous children lost to or affected by the residential school system.”




Kerry Saner-Harvey has been involved since the beginning. He noted that “age-appropriateness is important.”




He said that, until children reach a certain age, residential schools are not covered in depth.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Residential school survivor calls for understanding at annual Every Child Matters Powwow
content:
The steady thump of drums could be heard in the background as drum groups and dancers readied themselves for the procession leading to the Saskatoon Tribal Council’s Every Child Matters powwow in Saskatoon.




The powwow is held each year to honour residential school survivors and remember the children who never made it home.




About 700 dancers in all manner of regalia registered for the powwow, which organizers say is to help people understand what the orange shirt means to residential school survivors, and to provide a safe atmosphere to celebrate culture that was lost to the school system.




One elderly survivor, Irene Nippi of Kinistin Saulteaux First Nation, said she went to residential school “for a long time.”




“There were a lot of things that happened, like sexual abuse, physical abuse, emotional abuse, and spiritual abuse. And most of the women I went to school with, the children, either committed suicide or died of alcoholism because of what happened to us at residential school,” Nippi said.




“And that’s why for me, it matters because it’s intergenerational. I myself, went to residential school and I thought I was doing a good thing sending my children to residential school only to find out they went through the same thing.”

author: Karyn Pugliese
title: ‘We are enough’: Inuit share what reconciliation means in Ottawa
content:
For Inuit marking the National Day of Truth and Reconciliation (NDTR) at a gathering in Ottawa, healing was less about ceremony than a difficult question: what does reconciliation actually look like in everyday life? Especially in a city where some find themselves pushed to the margins.




Standing beside her daughter Sara, Sipporah Enuaraq made reconciliation personal.




“What is truth and reconciliation? What does it mean? To me, truth is what I went through as an individual, my life experiences. Truth is and was what we want through our lives,” said Enuaraq.




Around them, about 50 people had gathered at Isaruit Inuit Arts in Ottawa for the NDTR. But this was less a commemorative ceremony than a workshop — an opportunity for Inuit to talk to one another about what reconciliation means.




For Enuaraq, who was born in Kangirtugaapik, Nunavut, when it comes to reconciliation, the first difficulty is the word itself.




“What is reconciliation? It’s a Qallunaaq (white people) word, so it’s an English word, and it took me a while to understand what reconciliation really means,” she said.




Eventually, she came to a conclusion.




“Now I understand. It’s making things right for what we went through and to make things happen in a better way, and in the way of our people, our life, and our hardships and our pains, and our unshed tears. That’s reconciliation, in my opinion

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: For Kátł’odeeche Elder Doug Lamalice, healing means upholding dene culture
content:
Doug Lamalice’s mother, Sarah Elizabeth Lamalice, rarely spoke about her experience in Hay River Residential School.




Instead, Doug and his siblings grew up with questions.




He and his siblings wondered why their mother insists they wear certain clothes and follow strict rules at home.




“We always wondered why we had sidewall cuts on our hair,” Lamalice said. “We’d put on a white shirt and black pants and shoes and wear them all day until the evening service.”




It is only later that Lamalice began to understand the reasons behind his strict upbringing.




“When I think about that right now it reminds me of how she never talked about it,” he said.




St. Peter’s was an Anglican-run Residential school at the Hay River mission on the traditional territory of Kátł’odeeche First Nation (KFN).




It operated for more than 40 years before closing in 1937. Indigenous students were forcibly removed from their families and from communities as far away as Wrigley and Fort Norman N.W.T. and Fort Chipewyan, Alta.




The N.W.T. had the highest percentage of students in residential schools of any area in Canada. St. Peter’s was one of 14 colonial institutions in the territory.

author: Keelan Jacobs | Fraser Needham
title: Survivors’ Flag raised on Parliament Hill as Canada marks National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
content:
First Nations, Inuit and Métis residential school survivors raised the Survivors’ Flag on Parliament Hill Wednesday, on the traditional territory of the Anishinaabeg Algonquin People, to honour Survivors and the children who never came home.




The ceremony marked the 6th National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.




Survivors and Elders were joined by the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, leaders of national Indigenous organizations, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour and Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty.




The flag was first raised on the Hill in August 2022. It was created in consultation with Inuit, Mi’kmaq, Atikamekw, Cree, Ojibway, Dakota, Mohawk, Dene, Nuu-chah-nulth, Secwepemc and Métis Nation survivors.




Antoine Mountain, a First Nations survivor, said the flag is more than a symbol.




“Having spent 12 years in residential schools, I know the importance of remembering our shared history,” Mountain said. “The Survivors’ Flag is more than a symbol. It is a recognition of the experiences of survivors, a tribute to our power, and a reminder that reconciliation requires truth, understanding, and action.”




Bernard Andreason, an Inuit survivor, said the schools followed him into adult life.

title: 2 killed, another 2 injured on Tsawwassen territory according to police
content:
Two people have died in what Delta police in British Columbia are calling a “medical incident” in South Delta on Tsawwassen First Nation territory.




“Preliminary information indicates the driver of the involved vehicle may have experienced a medical emergency prior to the collision,” said the police in a statement. “Four pedestrians were struck and, tragically, two people have died as a result of their injuries.




“The remaining injured individuals were treated at the scene by BC Emergency Health Services and transported to hospital.




The incident is not related to the Truth and Reconciliation Walk that was taking place on Tsawwassen First Nation lands at the time, police said, and there is “no ongoing risk to public safety.”




The ceremony marking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation was ended and people were asked to leave.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Mark Carney is banking on economic reconciliation but critics say he’s not on track
content:
When Wilton Littlechild was co-chairing the landmark Truth and Reconciliation Commission more than a decade ago, he thought a lot about the idea of economic reconciliation and how it could help transform Indigenous communities.




“You may have the best ideas in the world but without a fundamental grounding and foundation to self-determination, you’re missing a very important part,” Littlechild said in an interview with The Canadian Press.




Littlechild said economic reconciliation is still the key to achieving reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians — but not in the way Prime Minister Mark Carney sees it.




The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, launched out of a legal settlement between the federal government and survivors of residential schools, was tasked with researching the history and legacy of those institutions. It was chaired by Littlechild, Murray Sinclair and Marie Wilson.




Between 1857 and 1996, 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to attend church-run, government-funded schools. They were barred from speaking their languages in institutions often rife with abuse and located far away from their families and communities.

author: APTN National News
title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on APTN National News
content:
The sixth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation is taking place on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, and in communities and Nations across the country.




The day honours survivors of the residential school system and those who never made it home.




From the 1800s until the mid ‘90s, approximately 150 years, 150,000 children were sent to state-sponsored institutions to be stripped of their language and culture. The schools were run by different church organizations.




On June 11, 2008, former prime minister Stephen Harper apologized. His government set up the Indian Residential School Settlement Agreement that offered compensation and established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, or TRC. 

Call to Action 80

 in its 2016 report called for the government to establish a statutory National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.




APTN National News host Dennis Ward is in Ottawa for the main ceremony with Tiar Wheatle will be guiding the show in our studio in Winnipeg.




The show will include reports from APTN journalists across the country.




Here are the times: 




Pre-show: 11:00 a.m. ET until 12:00 p.m. ET




Main ceremony on Parliament Hill is from 12 p.m. to 1:30 p.m.




APTN News post show runs from 1:30 p.m. to 2:00 p.m. ET

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Public Safety minister appoints full time correctional investigator
content:
The federal government has appointed the new head at the Office of the Correctional Investigator, it announced Tuesday.




This will be the permanent successor to Ivan Zinger, who took his early retirement in February 2026, two years before his position expired.




The position was left vacant for four months until Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree appointed an interim commissioner.




David Paradiso, the deputy Ombudsman in B.C. will take the seat on Oct. 13.




Canada’s correctional investigator works as an independent watchdog for the federal corrections system, investigating submitted complaints and concerns that have to do with living conditions, overpopulation, and several other issues faced by incarcerated people in federal prisons.




Paradiso has been the deputy 

British Columbia Ombudsperson

 since 2014, and, according to Canada, has “35 years of experience in public sector oversight, legal analysis, and independent investigations.”




According to the 

Forum of Canadian Ombudsman

, he helped establish the national Ombudsman for Canada Post and then spent time at the RCMP Public Complaint Commission.




He served as director of investigations with the Office of the Correctional Investigator [OCI] for six years and handled complaints and allegations from or concerning those in incarceration.

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon Women’s Coalition raises alarm over RCMP incident at Whitehorse shelter
content:
A women’s coalition in the Yukon says it has serious concerns about an alleged excessive use of force incident last month involving an RCMP officer and a woman accessing services at a Whitehorse shelter.




According to 

new details released last week

 by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, or ASIRT, which is investigating the 

Aug. 11 incident

, an RCMP officer dragged a woman out of the Whitehorse emergency shelter and left her outside on the sidewalk.




The details also state there were no beds available at the shelter for the woman to stay overnight.




The 

Yukon Women’s Coalition

, a group of 10 women-led and feminist not-for-profit organizations, said in a 

Sept. 28 release

 that it’s “deeply concerned” about the incident and the new details that have been released.




“The details released thus far are deeply troubling and raise serious concerns about the dignity, safety and human rights of the woman involved, as well as the treatment of people accessing emergency shelter and other essential services,” it states.




“We are particularly concerned by the reported treatment of the woman by the RCMP member under investigation, and all circumstances surrounding the incident, including the apparent lack of available safe shelter space. There are many unanswered questions; however, it seems clear that this person has been systematically failed,” it adds.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Expert on white nationalism in Canada disturbed, not surprised by demonstration at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc
content:
A public demonstration by the white nationalist group Second Sons of Canada on land near the Kamloops residential school site over the weekend sent shockwaves across the country. For people who study the group and others like it, it was not surprising.




“White Nationalism 3.0 has emerged as a unifying organizational model within Canada’s white supremacist ecosystem,” wrote Steven Rai in

 Tribe and Train

,

 a March 2026 article which examined “Canada’s new model of white supremacist mobilization.”




Photos circulating Sunday showed men in black clothing, white face coverings and matching caps on the 

Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc

 reserve, some with flags. A later image appears to show the same group on the Pacific Way overpass in Kamloops holding a banner that read “Got Bones?”




“Despite frequent rebranding and occasional infighting, groups that have adopted this model (including 

Second Sons

 of Canada and the so-called Active Clubs) share a common strategy, unifying a previously fractured movement. This has allowed them to foster sustained growth since their emergence in Canada in 2021,” Rai, a senior research manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue Canada (ISD), wrote. ISD provides ” threat detection, analysis and real-world strategies to combat terrorism, extremism and authoritarianism – in all their ideological forms,” according to its website.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Kebaowek Nation pulls out of nuclear consultations, saying other parties failed
content:
Kebaowek First Nation announced Tuesday that it is suspending consultations on the proposed nuclear waste dump near its territory after it says the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) and Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL) “failed to meet critical commitments.”




According to a press release from Kebaowek First Nation, CNSC and CNL informed Kebaowek leadership that they would “no longer fund the Nation’s participation costs as previously understood,” and also that they would “end their participation in the co-development of a consent-based agreement to support the process.”




In 

a decision in February 2025

, Federal Court Justice Julie Blackhawk found that the CNSC failed to consider the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in developing plans for nuclear waste dump in Kebaowek’s ancestral territory. Blackhawk ordered CNSC and CNL to consult with Kebaowek through an Indigenous-led Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) process. That FPIC process has also been suspended as a result of Kebaowek’s ending consultations.




In a statement emailed to APTN News, CNL representatives said they have engaged with Kebaowek and its representatives for 19 months in accordance with Federal Court instructions.

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Indian hospital survivors shape future of $385M foundation as northern claimants navigate compensation process
content:
For decades, Indigenous patients were sent to federally operated hospitals where they could be segregated from other patients and subjected to psychological, verbal, physical and sexual abuse; now, survivors are being asked what should happen next.




The Federal Court approved a settlement June 24, 2025, involving 33 Indian hospitals operated by the federal government at various times between 1936 and 1981.




The 

settlement

 provides individual compensation to eligible primary class members and establishes a $385.5 million foundation intended to support healing, research, education and commemoration.




The claims process and work to establish the foundation are happening at the same time, but they serve different purposes.




For northern claimants, accessing compensation can come with additional barriers.




Public awareness




Dr. Mike DeGagné, who is leading engagement sessions with the Indian Hospital Engagement Foundation for the future foundation, said Survivors have an opportunity to help shape what it should look like.




“If I go somewhere in Canada and I mention Indian residential schools, everybody sort of knows what I’m talking about, but if I say Indian hospitals, often they have no idea,” DeGagné said.




That lack of public awareness was a focus of a Yellowknife engagement session Sept. 22, one of a series being held across Canada.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Manitoba to purchase private campground near site of former residential school
content:
The Manitoba government is partnering with the province’s second-largest city to purchase a private campground where historical records show a cemetery for children who died at a residential school is located.




Premier Wab Kinew announced his government is working with the city of Brandon to acquire the Turtle Crossing Campground site, located south of the former Brandon Indian Residential School in western Manitoba.




A news release says the cemetery was used from 1985 to 1912 after the area was converted into a suburban park.




First Nations groups have long advocated for a search of the area to determine how many children were buried in the area and their identities.




Kinew says any future decisions regarding the site will be be done in consultation with residential school survivors, impacted First Nations and advocacy groups.




Chief Jennifer Bone of Sioux Valley Dakota Nation says any searches will be Indigenous-led and technical expertise and community knowledge will help guide the work.




“This is important work for our nation and for Indigenous Peoples across Canada,” she said in a joint statement with the province.




The First Nation previously worked with researchers to investigate unmarked graves at the former Brandon Indian Residential School.




It has said more than 50 are on the campground.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Indigenous services minister ‘disgusted and appalled’ after masked gathering on Tk’emlúps land
content:
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty says she is “absolutely disgusted and appalled” after seeing a photograph of masked men who appeared on Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc land Sunday, three days before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.




Gull-Masty, a Cree woman from Waswanipi and the first Indigenous person to hold the Indigenous Services portfolio, spoke at the National Indigenous Collaborative Housing Incorporated (NICHI) on Monday and was asked about the incident.




“I’m really disturbed by the level of comfort that I see in the behaviour that’s been carried out,” she said. “I haven’t had the opportunity to receive my briefing. I can’t comment on exactly what happened. I haven’t received the details of that activity yet.




“But I can confidently say that I’m absolutely disgusted and appalled.”




The white nationalist group, Second Sons Canada, gathered in Kamloops on Sunday. Photo: Facebook.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Elections Alberta reports more than 655,000 requests for special ballots for Oct. 19 referendum
content:
There appears to be high voter interest in the Alberta referendum on Oct. 19 which will decide whether the province should pursue the formal process to separate from Canada.




“We received approximately 658,000 requests for special ballots,” an Elections Alberta news release said. “This is more than 11 times as many requests as the 2023 Provincial General Election, where we received 59,589 special ballot requests.”




Elections Alberta attributed the increase to “the new availability of special ballot voting to all eligible electors without a reason, that voters must vote within their Electoral Division for Advance Vote or at their assigned location for Election Day, voter interest, and the number of questions electors must vote on.”




More than 82 per cent of the special ballots have been approved for fulfilment and mailing, it noted, with “0.7 per cent rejected either at application or on return, and nearly 100,000 have been received back and approved, and those electors marked as voted.”




It also expects the “total requests number will change as all final requests received before the deadline are entered into the system.”

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Sister of late Russell Woodhouse wants to set record straight on 1973 manslaughter charge: affidavit
content:
The younger sister of a First Nations man convicted of manslaughter in the 1970s has taken his case back to the Manitoba Court of Appeal 15 years after his death.




Russell Woodhouse, a member of Pinaymootang First Nation, was one of four to receive sentences following the 1973 Winnipeg murder of Ting Fong Chan.




While Woodhouse received 10 years in prison for manslaughter, his brother, Clarence Woodhouse; cousin, Brian Anderson; and fellow community member Allan Woodhouse (unrelated), were convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison.




Innocence Canada, a legal non-profit organization that advocates for the exoneration of individuals who have been wrongly convicted, began to file applications to review the murder cases in 2019.




In 2023, Anderson and Allan Woodhouse were acquitted. Clarence Woodhouse was acquitted soon after, in 2024.




Now, Lisa Anderson, Russel and Clarence’s youngest sister, is returning to the Court of Appeal to have the outstanding case reassessed.




Lisa chose to take his place in court as his next of kin. He died of cancer in 2011, and the two “were always very close and remained close” until his death, she wrote in an affidavit filed in Winnipeg on Thursday.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: CAP national chief says $3M cut of federal money came without notice
content:
The 

Congress of Aboriginal Peoples (CAP)

 says the federal government has unilaterally ended the Canada-CAP Political Accord and cut about $3 million a year in funding with no notice — a move National Chief Brendan Moore says has already damaged the organization’s ability to do policy work.




Moore spoke after CAP supporters marched on Parliament Hill to protest what the organization called the “Government of Canada’s unilateral decision to end the Canada-CAP Political Accord.”




The 2018 accord was signed under former prime minister Justin Trudeau after the Supreme Court of Canada’s 2016 Daniels decision, which confirmed that Métis and non-status Indians fall under federal jurisdiction. 




CAP, founded in the 1970s, is one of five national Indigenous organizations recognized by Ottawa and says it represents Métis, status and non-status First Nations people, and southern Inuit living off reserve.




“Canada has terminated its participation in the Canada-CAP Political Accord. There was no consultation with us. There was no replacement mechanism offered,” Moore said.




He said the cut landed all at once.




“It does really damage our capacity to do policy work,” he said. “For the first time in the history of CAP we never qualified for the Federal Interlocutor’s Contribution Program.”




Moore, left, marching with supporters on Parliament Hill. Photo: Keelan Jacobs/A

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Selon des historiens autochtones, l’histoire du Québec présentée par le PQ est trompeuse
content:
Le Parti québécois (PQ) est en voie de remporter les prochaines élections provinciales du 5 octobre, et s’il y parvient, il a promis d’organiser un référendum sur l’indépendance du Québec vis-à-vis du Canada dès son premier mandat – mais il n’a pas beaucoup parlé de la place qu’occuperaient les Premières Nations et les Inuit dans ce projet.




Pendant l’année, le PQ a publié des chapitres de 

son « Livre bleu »

, un plan officiel décrivant le fonctionnement d’un Québec indépendant.




Cependant, le chapitre 22, intitulé « Relations avec les Premières Nations et les Inuit », n’est pour l’instant qu’une page blanche, accompagnée de la promesse que ce chapitre serait publié « au cours de l’été 2026 ».




APTN News a contacté le PQ pour savoir si ce chapitre était disponible, mais n’a reçu aucune réponse.




Même s’il n’y a encore rien dans le chapitre 22, le Livre bleu du PQ présente tout de même une version de l’histoire des relations entre les Français et les peuples autochtones au Québec.




Scott Berthelette, professeur métis de la Rivière-Rouge, étudie les relations entre les Français et les peuples autochtones en Nouvelle-France à l’université Queen’s. Il estime que le récit du Livre bleu du PQ simplifie à l’extrême une histoire complexe impliquant de nombreuses nations, chacune avec des intérêts différents, nouant des alliances multiples et menant des guerres.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: PQ’s history of Quebec is misleading: Indigenous historians
content:
The Parti Québécois (PQ) is poised to win the upcoming provincial election on Oct. 5, and if they do, they have promised to call a referendum on Quebec’s independence from Canada within the first term – yet they’ve said little about how First Nations and Inuit fit into that plan. 

 




Over the past year, the PQ has been publishing chapters of 

its “Blue Book,”

 a formal plan for how an independent Quebec would function. 




However, Chapter 22, “Relations with First Nations and Inuit,” is currently a blank page with the promise that the chapter would be published “sometime in the summer of 2026.”

 




APTN News contacted the PQ to find out whether the chapter was available and received no response.







While there is nothing yet in Chapter 22, the PQ Blue Book nonetheless presents a version of the history between the French and Indigenous Peoples in Quebec.




Red River Métis history professor Scott Berthelette studies French–Indigenous relations in New France at Queen’s University. He sees the PQ Blue Book’s narrative as dramatically simplifying a complex history of many nations, each with different interests, entering multiple alliances and waging wars.

 




Berthelette told APTN that he noted in the PQ Blue Book a desire to mark the British as bad, while tying modern Francophone society in Quebec to roots predating the English conquest of Quebec.

author: Mark Blackburn
title: NAFC says friendship centres laying off staff, need $25M extra from Ottawa
content:
The head of the 

National Association of Friendship Centres

 (NAFC) says the organization needs more money to meet the needs of urban Indigenous people across the country.




At a news conference in Ottawa this week, CEO Jennifer Rankin said the lack of sustainable funding has had an effect on a number of centres.




“With this new government, there’s some education that’s needed from within, said Rankin. “Teaching people the realities of Indigenous people throughout Canada, urban Indigenous realities and letting them know and educating them on friendship centres and what we do and how we contribute to the Canadian economy and how we already are.




“The reality on that, being fiscally responsible, there were some executive directors who did have to do layoffs,” said Rankin. “We tried to cost manage and support most of our friendship centres.”




Rankin didn’t know how many people have been laid off.




Friendship Centres are the country’s largest urban Indigenous service network with more than 100 serving nearly one million people a year through employment and training, housing help, child care, health supports, cultural programming and food security.
